# C — Configuration

Use this file to rate each item from the code and configuration. The requirement is the checklist text. The heuristics say what to look for. Ratings: likely_pass, gap, needs_evidence, or na_candidate. Never rate pass.

## C01 · G2 · C1–C6/Obs-T1 — Complete release manifest

**Lead:** Agent team. **Shares:** Infrastructure, Model team, Data and privacy.

### Requirement

Write a release manifest: a list of everything that makes up this release. Include the container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, and execution budgets. Include security-policy versions. Add a separate model record for every model: the main agent model, sub-agent models, and helper models such as embedding models and rerankers. For each, record the provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and any adapter or fine-tune version. For training or fine-tuning you run yourself, also record the training job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and the digest of the output. The agent app's release number alone is not enough. Use the [model provenance fields](CHECKLIST-VERIFICATION.md#model-provenance-fields) to separate recorded versions from details a provider doesn't share. Check each model ID you request against the provider's versioning docs. Mark it as a pinned snapshot or as an alias that can change, and record which doc you used and its date. Naming rules differ by provider and model generation. Name each artifact's owner and a reference that can't change, where one exists. A machine-readable format, such as CycloneDX ML-BOM or the SPDX 3.0 AI and Dataset profiles, lets tools check the manifest.

  Why this is hard: Teams can usually find their own training jobs and datasets. A hosted provider may not share its pretraining runs, weights, or data versions. Separate the records your team should have from the details the provider keeps private.

  If you can't fully do it: Fill in model records from serving metadata, registries, and training-job output. Require full history for training your team runs. Clearly label fields the provider hides, and keep where and when you checked. Prefer a fixed provider snapshot when one exists. Record missing training history your team should have as a Gap, and rebuild it first. Never make up training versions. Never treat a provider alias as a training job ID.

  Tradeoffs you can accept: Provider pretraining details that are clearly marked as not shared, as long as your own model-selection and training records are complete. A G2 gap in visibility or history can get written acceptance with an owner. Unknown records must never be written down as real versions.

### Verification recipe

Export the deployed artifacts and settings, and match them field by field against the manifest. Fill in the provenance fields above for every model role. For each training job you ran, follow its output digest to the served checkpoint or adapter. Separate fields the provider doesn't share from records your team is missing. Check each requested model ID's snapshot-or-alias label against the cited provider doc.

**Evidence to keep:** Manifest-vs-deployment diff, model registry records, training jobs, dataset versions.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C01.1** A release manifest file lists the container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, execution budgets, and security-policy versions. *(A document can show this.)*
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find the release manifest (`.brace/manifest.yaml`, release manifest, ML-BOM). 2) Check each category: container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval, identity bindings, network rules, budgets, security-policy versions. 3) Compare with what config sets up (`*.mcp.json`, NetworkPolicy). 4) Answer no if any category is missing or configured items are left out.
- **C01.2** The manifest has a separate model record for every model (main, sub-agent, and helper models such as embedding models and rerankers), each with provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and adapter or fine-tune version. *(A document can show this.)*
  - *How to verify:* 1) Search code for every model used: main, sub-agent, embedding, reranker, judge. 2) Check the manifest has a separate record for each. 3) Check each record has provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and adapter or fine-tune version. 4) Answer no if any model in code has no record, or a record is missing a field.
- **C01.3** Each requested model ID is labeled as a pinned snapshot or a changeable alias, with the provider doc and date used.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open each model record in the manifest. 2) Check it has a pinned-or-alias label, the provider doc used, and a date. 3) Answer no if any record lacks one of these, or labels an undated or `-latest` name as pinned.
- **C01.4** Each artifact has a named owner and a reference that can't change (digest or commit) where one exists, not a mutable tag or the app's release number.
  - *How to verify:* 1) For each manifest artifact, check for a named owner. 2) Check its reference is a digest (`sha256:`) or commit SHA where one exists. 3) Answer no if any artifact has no owner, or uses a mutable tag (`:latest`, branch name) or the app release number where a digest or commit was available.
- **C01.5** For training the team runs itself, the manifest records the training job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and output digest.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Search for training or fine-tuning code (training jobs, `Trainer`, fine-tune API calls, pipeline configs). 2) If found, check the manifest records job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and output digest. 3) Answer no if training runs here and any field is missing. Answer unknown if training may run in another repo.

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- A release manifest file listing container digest, harness version, system prompt and rules files, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, execution budgets, and security-policy versions.
- A separate model record for each model role (main, sub-agent, judge, embedding, reranker) with provider, requested model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and adapter or fine-tune version.
- Each requested model ID marked as pinned snapshot or changeable alias, with the provider doc and date cited.
- For self-run training: job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and output digest.
- Owners named per artifact, and immutable references (digests, commit SHAs) where they exist; optionally a CycloneDX ML-BOM or SPDX 3.0 AI profile.

**Red flags:**
- Only an app version number or git tag identifies the release.
- Helper models (embedding, reranker, judge) are missing from the manifest.
- Provider alias written into a training job or version field, or made-up version values where the provider shares none.
- MCP servers, egress rules, or budgets are configured but not listed in the manifest.
- Model ID recorded with no pinned-or-alias label.

**Where to look:**
- .brace/manifest.yaml, release manifests, SBOM/ML-BOM files (`*.cdx.json`, `bom.json`)
- model config files and env vars that set model IDs
- *.mcp.json, agent config, k8s NetworkPolicy, Helm values
- training pipeline configs and model registry references

## C02 · G2 · C1–C7 — Review security-relevant changes

**Lead:** Governance. **Shares:** Agent team, Security.

### Requirement

Require diffs with a named author, plus review, for changes to the manifest and its policies. Show who is allowed to change production config. Record emergency changes with an owner, a reason, an end date, and a follow-up review.

### Verification recipe

Use a role without release permission to try changing a prompt, a tool, and a network policy. Each change must be denied. Review one normal change and one controlled emergency change. Check for a named approver, an end date where needed, and a follow-up review.

**Evidence to keep:** Role policy, rejected edits, normal and emergency change records.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C02.1** The manifest, prompts, tool config, and policy files live in version control, and merges require review by someone other than the named author.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Check the manifest, prompts, tool config, and policy files are tracked in git, not loaded at runtime from an untracked path or remote URL. 2) Look for branch protection or ruleset config requiring approving review, and CODEOWNERS covering those paths. 3) Answer no if any of these files is untracked or not covered. Answer unknown if review rules are set only in the hosting service.
- **C02.2** Only named roles in config (CODEOWNERS, IAM, or protected CI environments) can change production configuration.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open CODEOWNERS, IAM policies, and CI environment config (protected `environment:` entries). 2) Check production config paths and deploy jobs are limited to named roles. 3) Answer no if a catch-all `*` owner, a broad group, or the agent's own credentials can change production config, or a deploy job skips the protected environment.
- **C02.3** An emergency change path exists that records an owner, a reason, an end date, and a follow-up review.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Search for an emergency or break-glass path (runbook, workflow, CLI). 2) Check it records owner, reason, end date, and follow-up review. 3) Answer no if any of the four is missing, or the path bypasses review with no record. Answer unknown if the procedure lives outside this repo.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Running config drifting from the approved baseline unnoticed → **C04**
- Release candidate not re-tested against attack cases → **C06**
- No tested rollback to an approved setup → **C07**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- Branch protection and CODEOWNERS requiring review on prompts, tool configs, manifest, and policy files.
- Production config deploys only through CI/CD (GitOps, pipeline approvals), not manual edits.
- IAM or RBAC that limits who can change production config, prompts, and network policy.
- A documented emergency-change path that records owner, reason, end date, and follow-up review.

**Red flags:**
- Prompts or tool lists loaded from a database, admin UI, or feature-flag service that anyone with app access can edit without review.
- CODEOWNERS or required reviews missing for prompt, policy, or MCP config paths.
- Deploy scripts or `kubectl apply` run from laptops with broad production credentials.
- Break-glass access with no expiry or no follow-up record.

**Where to look:**
- CODEOWNERS, branch protection settings, `.github/workflows` or other CI configs
- prompt storage (files vs database vs remote prompt registry)
- IAM/RBAC for deploy roles; GitOps config (Argo CD, Flux)
- change-management or break-glass docs

**Needs runtime evidence:** Needs the C02 recipe: try changing a prompt, tool, and network policy with a role lacking release permission and see each denied, and review real normal and emergency change records.

**N/A when:** never

## C03 · G1 · Obs-T1 — Match release identity to running state

**Lead:** Infrastructure. **Shares:** Agent team, Operations, Model team.

### Requirement

Freeze the artifacts that define identity for each release. Check the running setup against the approved manifest, and emit the matching agent-type-id. Include the digest and signature of weights and adapters you host yourself. Test that a changed prompt, model, weights file, or tool setup can't keep showing the old approved identity without being caught.

  Why this is hard: A manifest or an ID the agent reports about itself can stay the same while the running prompt, tool setup, or hosted model changes. You may not be able to inspect a provider's internals yourself.

  If you can't fully do it: Observe local artifacts and deployment settings yourself, not from what the agent reports, and compare them with the manifest. Block or quarantine any mismatch you find. Check the served model's metadata when the provider shares it. Limit the claim to artifacts you control and provider references you can see. Track hidden remote state under C05. A provider's limits never excuse an unchecked local setup. Changed local artifacts must never keep their approved identity unnoticed.

  Tradeoffs you can accept: Checks limited to artifacts you control and provider references you can see, with hidden remote state handled under C05. More frequent checks may cost time and compute. Unchecked local artifacts, or unnoticed changes to declared local settings, still block release.

### Verification recipe

Compare the runtime artifact references you observe yourself with the approved manifest and the type ID the agent emits. In a test deployment, swap in a different prompt, model, self-hosted weights file, or tool setup. The mismatch must be caught or rejected. Don't trust the ID the agent reports about itself.

**Evidence to keep:** Runtime export, manifest comparison, mismatch event.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C03.1** Identity-defining artifacts are referenced in deployment config by digest or a version that can't change, not by mutable tags.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open deployment config: Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, Terraform, compose files. 2) Check images use `@sha256:` and prompts, models, and weights use fixed versions. 3) Follow variables and defaults to the final value. 4) Answer no if any reference is a tag like `:latest`, a branch, a model alias, or a default that falls back to one.
- **C03.2** A process outside the agent observes the running artifacts (image digest, prompt, model, tool setup) and compares them with the approved manifest, rather than trusting what the agent reports.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find a process outside the agent (admission controller, CI check, sidecar, scheduled job) that reads running artifacts. 2) Check it observes image digest, prompt, model, and tool setup itself and compares each with the approved manifest. 3) Answer no if it trusts values the agent reports, or compares a value with itself. Answer unknown if it would run in a platform outside this repo.
- **C03.3** The emitted agent-type-id is computed from the observed running artifacts, so a changed prompt, model, weights file, or tool setup produces a different ID instead of the approved one.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find where the emitted `agent.type.id` comes from. 2) Check it is computed from the observed running artifacts at start or deploy. 3) Answer no if it is a constant, an env var or config value set at build, or copied from the approved manifest, so a changed prompt, model, weights file, or tool setup would still emit the approved ID.
- **C03.4** Self-hosted weights and adapters are checked by digest and signature at load or deploy.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find where self-hosted weights and adapters are loaded or deployed (`from_pretrained`, `torch.load`, `safetensors`, download steps). 2) Check a digest compare and a signature check run before use. 3) Answer no if either is missing, wrapped in `try/except` that continues, or a second load path skips it. If only hosted models are used, answer yes citing the config that shows that.
- **C03.5** A mismatch blocks or quarantines the deployment, not only logs it.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find the code that handles a manifest or digest mismatch. 2) Check it blocks or quarantines: non-zero exit, admission deny, refusal to start, scale to zero. 3) Answer no if the mismatch branch only logs, warns, or emits a metric and continues, or an error in the check lets deployment proceed.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Manifest missing helper models, budgets, or other components → **C01**
- Hosted model changing behind a fixed name → **C05**
- Agent-type-id not computed as a hash of its identity inputs → **A03**
- Container image not signature-checked at admission → **B10**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- A deploy-time or startup check that compares running artifacts (image digest, prompt hash, model ID, tool config, weights digest) with the approved manifest and fails on mismatch.
- The emitted `agent.type.id` is computed from the artifacts actually loaded, not read from a static config value.
- Admission control that verifies image signatures and digests (for example Sigstore policy-controller, Kyverno, Gatekeeper).
- Self-hosted weights and adapters checked against digest and signature before load.

**Red flags:**
- `agent.type.id` is a constant in config or env that stays the same when the prompt or model changes.
- Prompts or tool definitions fetched at runtime from a mutable source with no hash check.
- Images deployed by mutable tag with no digest verification.
- The only check is the agent reporting its own ID.

**Where to look:**
- startup and bootstrap code in the harness
- CI/CD deploy steps and admission policies
- model loading code for self-hosted weights
- prompt and tool config loaders

**Needs runtime evidence:** Needs the C03 recipe: observe runtime artifact references independently, compare to the manifest and emitted ID, and swap a prompt, model, weights file, or tool setup in a test deployment to show the mismatch is caught.

**N/A when:** never

## C04 · G2 · C1/C3/C4/Obs-T1 — Detect drift per agent

**Lead:** Operations. **Shares:** Infrastructure, Security, Model team.

### Requirement

Compare running images, harness settings, prompts, MCP server lists, permissions, network policies, and self-hosted model weights against their approved baseline. Simulate a prompt edit, an added tool, and a looser egress rule. Check that each one raises an alert and gets the documented response — block, quarantine, or rollback — within a set time.

### Verification recipe

In a separate deployment, change the prompt, the MCP server list, and the egress policy one at a time, outside the approved baseline. Measure how long detection and response take. Every change must trigger the documented action within the agreed time.

**Evidence to keep:** State before and after, drift alerts, quarantine or rollback events.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C04.1** A drift check compares running images, harness settings, prompts, MCP server lists, permissions, network policies, and self-hosted model weights against the approved baseline, with each of these covered.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find the drift check job or tool. 2) List what it compares: images, harness settings, prompts, MCP server lists, permissions, network policies, self-hosted weights. 3) Check each is compared with the approved baseline, not with the live state itself. 4) Answer no if any category is missing or excluded. Answer unknown if drift detection runs in an outside platform.
- **C04.2** The drift check runs per agent deployment, on a schedule or on change events.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find what triggers the drift check: cron or CI schedule, admission webhook, or change events. 2) Check it runs for each agent deployment, not once for the fleet or only by hand. 3) Answer no if it is manual-only or covers only some deployments. Answer unknown if scheduling is set outside this repo.
- **C04.3** Detected drift triggers an alert and a set response (block, quarantine, or rollback) defined in config, with a time limit.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open the drift check's result handling. 2) Check drift raises an alert and triggers a response set in config: block, quarantine, or rollback. 3) Check a time limit is set. 4) Answer no if drift only logs, the response or time limit is missing, or a check error is treated as no drift.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Hosted model changing behind a fixed name → **C05**
- A tool server changing its description or schema after approval → **E03**
- Who may change production config, and emergency change records → **C02**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- A drift detector that compares running images, harness settings, prompts, MCP server lists, permissions, network policies, and self-hosted weights against a baseline per agent.
- GitOps self-heal or drift alerts (for example Argo CD out-of-sync alerts, Terraform drift checks, cloud config rules).
- Alert rules that route drift to a named response: block, quarantine, or rollback, with a time target.

**Red flags:**
- Drift checks cover infrastructure only, not prompts, MCP server lists, or tool config.
- Drift alerts exist but have no owner, no response action, or no time target.

## C05 · G2 · C3/C4/C7 — Control dependency, model, and training changes

**Lead:** Agent team. **Shares:** Model team, Security, Vendors.

### Requirement

Pin dependency versions. Where supported, also pin each model's base version, checkpoint or weights, and fine-tune or adapter version. Before promotion, link any changed training run, dataset, or training code or config to the model it produced and to its test results. Record the model version actually served, when the runtime or provider shares it, separately from the name you requested. Before loading weights, adapters, or datasets you host, check their signature against an approved signer (for example, with OpenSSF Model Signing). Also check their file format. Pickle-based formats can run code when loaded, so they need an approved exception and a scan. Test swapping a model, checkpoint, or adapter, and check that it triggers review and re-testing. Some remote services or names can change behind a fixed name. For those, record missing training and version details clearly. Watch available version metadata and provider notices, and decide when to re-test or stop using the model. A local config hash alone can't prove remote behavior is unchanged. A pinned snapshot fixes the weights, not the provider's serving systems, which can change under the same ID. Keep scheduled re-testing.

  Why this is hard: A hosted service may change behind a name without sharing a version ID or training history. Behavior tests can catch some changes, but they can't prove nothing hidden changed.

  If you can't fully do it: Prefer pinned snapshots. Otherwise keep both the requested and the observed IDs, watch provider notices, and schedule realistic tests with a named owner. Limit permissions and autonomy while you're unsure of the version. Decide in advance what triggers a pause or a move to an approved alternative. Record gaps from names that can change, and any allowed risk acceptance. Tests and provider notices help manage uncertainty. They don't prove the model's identity is fixed.

  Tradeoffs you can accept: The ease of a hosted model, with less reproducibility and possibly slower detection of changes, once that exposure has written G2 acceptance. Set a testing schedule and decide when use must stop. If the uncertainty matters too much, choose a pinned alternative or reduce the agent's powers.

### Verification recipe

Replace a checkpoint or adapter, and confirm promotion requires review and testing. Load a weights folder with one changed file and one added file. Also load an unsigned or pickle-based artifact that has no approved exception. Loading must be refused. For training you run, trace a changed dataset, code, or config through a new run to its output. For hosted aliases, test a change in served-version metadata when the provider shares it. Otherwise, run the documented process for provider notices or scheduled re-testing, and record what it can't detect.

**Evidence to keep:** Version diffs, training-to-output history, promotion block, provider monitoring record.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C05.1** Dependency versions are pinned with exact versions or hashes in lockfiles, with no ranges or floating tags.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open every dependency file and lockfile (`requirements*.txt`, `poetry.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `go.sum`) plus Dockerfile `FROM` and install lines. 2) Look for ranges (`^`, `~`, `>=`, `*`), missing lockfiles, and floating tags. 3) Answer no if any dependency is unpinned, including install commands in Dockerfiles or CI scripts that bypass the lockfile.
- **C05.2** Model IDs in config are pinned snapshots (plus checkpoint, weights, and adapter versions where supported), not aliases such as 'latest'.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find every model ID in config, env files, and code defaults. 2) Follow env vars to their fallback value. 3) Answer no if any is an alias (`-latest`, undated name), falls back to one when unset, or leaves out the checkpoint, weights, or adapter version where one is used and the provider supports pinning it.
- **C05.3** Self-hosted weights, adapters, and datasets have their signatures checked against an approved signer before loading, and loading stops if the check fails.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find load paths for self-hosted weights, adapters, and datasets. 2) Check a signature check against an approved signer (for example OpenSSF Model Signing, `cosign verify` with a pinned identity) runs before loading. 3) Answer no if any path skips it, any signer is accepted, or a failure is caught and loading continues. If nothing is self-hosted, answer yes citing the config that shows that.
- **C05.4** Pickle-based model formats are refused at load unless an approved exception and scan are recorded.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Search for pickle-capable loads: `pickle.load`, `torch.load`, `joblib.load`, `.pkl`, `.pt`, `.bin` files. 2) Check the loader refuses these formats unless an approved exception and scan are recorded. 3) Answer no if any pickle-based load runs without that check.
- **C05.5** The model version the provider or runtime reports serving is recorded separately from the requested model name.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find model call sites and their response handling. 2) Check the served version from the response or runtime (for example the response `model` field) is stored in its own field. 3) Answer no if only the requested name is recorded, or the served field is filled with the requested value.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Tool or MCP server approved without reviewing publisher, permissions, or vulnerabilities → **E02**
- Container image not pinned by digest or signature-checked → **B10**
- Rollback setup naming a hosted model that is retired → **C07**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- Lockfiles with exact versions or hashes for dependencies (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, `go.sum`).
- Model IDs pinned to dated or snapshot versions where the provider offers them; requested and served model versions both logged.
- Weights, adapters, and datasets you host are signature-checked against an approved signer (for example OpenSSF Model Signing) before load.
- Safe formats (for example safetensors) required; pickle-based loads blocked unless there is an approved exception and scan.
- Promotion gates that link a changed training run, dataset, or training config to the produced model and its test results; scheduled re-tests for aliases.

**Red flags:**
- Model alias like `-latest` or an unversioned family name in production config.
- `torch.load`, `pickle.load`, or `trust_remote_code=True` on weights with no signature check or exception record.
- Dependencies with ranges (`^`, `~`, `>=`) and no lockfile.
- Weights or adapters downloaded at startup from a hub by name with no revision or digest pin.
- Response metadata with the served model version is discarded.

**Where to look:**
- lockfiles and dependency manifests
- model config and env vars for model IDs
- model and adapter loading code
- training pipelines and promotion workflows

**Needs runtime evidence:** Code shows pinning and load checks. The C05 recipe proves a swapped checkpoint triggers review, changed or unsigned weights are refused, and the provider notice or re-test process runs. Hidden provider changes behind a fixed ID can't be proven from code.

**N/A when:** never

## C06 · G2 · C4–C9 — Re-test changed behavior

**Lead:** Agent team. **Shares:** Security, Business owner.

### Requirement

Before promotion, run typical allowed tasks and attack cases against the release candidate. Include destructive-action denial, access limits, injection containment, audit attribution, and stopping. Include retrieval, memory, and checker tests where they apply. If misalignment is in scope, include attempts to slip past monitoring and the stop path. Keep the results for the exact candidate manifest.

### Verification recipe

Run the release test suite for the exact candidate and model artifacts. Include allowed tasks and the attack cases from this guide that apply. If misalignment is in scope, include attempts to slip past monitoring and the stop path. Compare results to pass criteria set in advance. Block promotion on any blocking failure.

**Evidence to keep:** Suite version, candidate manifest and model IDs, results, release-gate decision.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C06.1** A CI release gate runs the test suite against the exact candidate (manifest digest and model IDs), with pass criteria set before the run, and blocks promotion on any blocking failure.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open the CI workflow for release or promotion. 2) Check it runs the suite against the candidate's manifest digest and model IDs, with pass criteria in config before the run. 3) Check promotion depends on it. 4) Answer no if the job uses `continue-on-error`, `|| true`, or allowed failures, tests a different build, or promotion can run without it.
- **C06.2** The suite includes cases for destructive-action denial, access limits, injection containment, audit attribution, and stopping, plus retrieval, memory, and checker tests where these apply.
  - *How to verify:* 1) List the test cases in the release suite. 2) Check each category exists: destructive-action denial, access limits, injection containment, audit attribution, stopping, plus retrieval, memory, and checker tests where those features exist. 3) Answer no if any category is missing or its tests are skipped (`skip`, `xfail`, excluded markers).
- **C06.3** Test results are stored linked to the exact candidate manifest.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find where CI stores test results (artifacts, uploads, database). 2) Check each result is tagged with the candidate's manifest digest or type ID. 3) Answer no if results stay only in CI logs, are tagged only by branch or build number, or are not stored.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Running config drifting from the approved baseline unnoticed → **C04**
- No tested rollback to an approved setup → **C07**
- Config changes made without a reviewed diff and named author → **C02**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- A release test suite in CI that runs allowed tasks plus attack cases: destructive-action denial, access limits, injection containment, audit attribution, and stopping.
- Retrieval, memory, and checker tests where those features exist; monitoring-evasion and stop-path tests if misalignment is in scope.
- Pass criteria defined in advance in config or test code.
- The release pipeline blocks promotion on any blocking failure and stores results keyed to the candidate manifest and model IDs.

**Red flags:**
- Eval jobs marked `continue-on-error` or allowed to fail without blocking deploy.
- Only happy-path or quality evals; no attack or denial cases.
- Tests run against a mocked model or a different model ID than the release candidate.
- Results not stored or not tied to a specific manifest.

**Where to look:**
- CI workflows and release pipelines
- eval and test directories (red-team suites, promptfoo, inspect, pytest suites)
- release gate scripts

**Needs runtime evidence:** Needs the C06 run: suite version, candidate manifest and model IDs, results, and the gate decision for the exact release candidate.

**N/A when:** never

## C07 · G2 · C8/C9 — Rollback and restart

**Lead:** Operations. **Shares:** Agent team, Infrastructure.

### Requirement

Keep an approved recovery setup and show that rollback works. Confirm each hosted model it names is still offered, and record the announced retirement date. Account for changed credentials, memory and index state, checkpoints, and queued work. Don't restore revoked permissions or replay unsafe side effects just because the old artifact still exists.

### Verification recipe

Upgrade a test deployment, create pending work and a revoked credential, then roll back. Confirm the approved old artifact runs and each hosted model it names is still offered. Confirm the credential stays revoked. Confirm queues, memory, search state, and side effects match the recovery procedure.

**Evidence to keep:** Rollback events, actual permissions, state and queue comparison.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C07.1** An approved recovery setup is defined with references that can't change, and a rollback procedure or pipeline exists in code.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find the recovery setup: a pinned earlier manifest or release record. 2) Check its references are digests or fixed versions. 3) Find a rollback script, pipeline, or runbook in the repo. 4) Answer no if references are tags or aliases, or no rollback procedure exists.
- **C07.2** Credentials and permission grants are managed apart from the rolled-back artifacts, so a rollback does not restore revoked access.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open the rollback procedure. 2) Check what it restores. 3) Answer no if it re-applies IAM policies, RoleBindings, secrets, or API keys from the old release, so revoked access comes back. Answer unknown if credentials are managed in another system and the repo does not show how.
- **C07.3** The rollback procedure handles memory and index state, checkpoints, and queued work explicitly (drain, migrate, or discard), so unsafe side effects are not replayed.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open the rollback procedure. 2) Look for explicit steps for memory and index state, checkpoints, and queued work: drain, migrate, or discard. 3) Answer no if any of these is not handled, or queued work is replayed as-is.
- **C07.4** Each hosted model named in the recovery setup has a recorded retirement date. *(A document can show this.)*
  - *How to verify:* 1) List the hosted models named in the recovery setup. 2) Check each has a recorded retirement date. 3) Answer no if any hosted model lacks one.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Changed or tampered checkpoints accepted, or unsafe replay of actions → **R14**
- Hosted model changing behind a fixed name → **C05**
- Stop doesn't halt running work or open tool streams within a set time → **R11**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- A documented rollback procedure and an approved previous release kept available (prior image digests, prior manifest).
- Rollback steps that handle credentials, memory and index state, checkpoints, and queued work.
- Revocations stored outside the release artifact so a rollback does not restore them.
- Retirement dates recorded for each hosted model the recovery release names.

**Red flags:**
- Rollback redeploys an old manifest that includes credentials or permissions since revoked.
- Queued jobs replay automatically after rollback with no check for already-done side effects.
- Recovery release names a hosted model with no check that it is still offered.
- No retained artifact for the previous release (images overwritten by tag).

**Where to look:**
- runbooks and rollback scripts
- deploy pipeline rollback stages, Helm history, GitOps revisions
- queue and memory/index migration code
- secret and credential management config

**Needs runtime evidence:** Needs the C07 drill: upgrade, create pending work and a revoked credential, roll back, and confirm the credential stays revoked and state and queues match the procedure.

**N/A when:** never

## C08 · G2 · Obs-T1/Obs-T2/Obs-T3 — Connect configuration to execution

**Lead:** Operations. **Shares:** Agent team, Infrastructure.

### Requirement

From a trace, look up the release manifest, the context sizes at each decision, and any prompts a parent passed to a sub-agent. Keep these links for the full audit retention period. Control access to sensitive artifacts.

### Verification recipe

Pick a past trace. Using the incident-response role, pull its manifest, model records, context sizes, and any prompts passed from a parent. Confirm these links stay available for the required retention period under the storage policy.

**Evidence to keep:** Lookup results, retention and access settings, missing-link check.

### Checks for likely_pass

Rate likely_pass only if every check below is true, with a file and line for each:

- **C08.1** Each trace or audit record carries the agent-type-id or manifest reference that resolves to the stored release manifest.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Open the trace or audit record writer. 2) Check every record carries `agent.type.id` or a manifest reference. 3) Check that value is the key of a stored manifest. 4) Answer no if the field is missing on some paths (errors, background jobs) or holds a value that resolves to no stored manifest.
- **C08.2** The context size at each model decision is recorded in the trace.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find model call sites and their spans. 2) Look for the context size recorded per call (for example `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` or a context-length attribute). 3) Answer no if it is missing on any model call path, including retries and sub-agents.
- **C08.3** Prompts passed from a parent to a sub-agent are stored and linked from the trace.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find sub-agent spawn code. 2) Check the parent's prompt is stored and the trace holds a link to it (ID, hash, or URI). 3) Answer no if the prompt is not stored, prompt capture is off, or the trace has no link.
- **C08.4** Storage config keeps manifests, traces, and these links for at least the audit retention period, and limits access to sensitive artifacts by role.
  - *How to verify:* 1) Find storage config for manifests, traces, and prompt links: bucket lifecycle rules, log retention, TTLs. 2) Check retention covers the audit period for all of them. 3) Check IAM limits sensitive artifacts by role. 4) Answer no if any has a shorter TTL, no retention, or broad read access. Answer unknown if storage is configured outside this repo.

### Not covered here

File these problems under their owning item, not this one, unless this item's own requirement is also broken:

- Context size not measured or logged for each action decision → **R07**
- Action records missing any of the six identity fields → **A02**
- Manifest missing components that define the release → **C01**

### Heuristics

**Provable from code:** partly

**Look for:**
- Traces carry `agent.type.id` linking to a stored manifest, `agent.context.size` per decision, and `agent.parent.prompt` (or its hash reference) for sub-agents.
- Manifest archive keyed by type ID with retention at least as long as the audit retention period.
- Storage policies (bucket lifecycle, log retention settings) that match the required retention.
- Access controls on sensitive artifacts such as prompts and parent prompts.

**Red flags:**
- `agent.context.size` missing, or emitted as zero when unknown.
- Manifests or prompts kept for less time than traces, so old traces can't be resolved.
- Trace retention set to a short default (for example 7 or 30 days) with no longer audit export.
- Sensitive prompt artifacts readable by everyone with log access.

**Where to look:**
- OpenTelemetry instrumentation and exporter config
- log and trace backend retention settings, bucket lifecycle rules
- manifest storage and artifact registry config

**Needs runtime evidence:** Needs the C08 recipe: from a past trace, pull the manifest, model records, context sizes, and parent prompts with the incident-response role, and confirm retention settings.

**N/A when:** never
